Final readouts & learned weights ↓

Play stops after each complete layer. Continue to the next, or Restart from the beginning. Reduce animations advances one exact gate per click; the slider and milestones reach the full circuit.

Why does a vector shrink inside the sphere?

A qubit entangled with other wires generally has a mixed reduced state. Its Bloch vector can be shorter than one even though the full circuit remains a pure state. We compute ρq = Tr(other wires)|ψ⟩⟨ψ| and plot (TrρX, TrρY, TrρZ). A CNOT is shown at its exact before/after endpoints; the linking pulse is an illustration of the gate.

From a descriptor to a quantum rotation ↓

Each classical descriptor x lies between 0 and 1. Encoding uses an angle α = πx. For a qubit initially at |0⟩, RY(α)|0⟩ = cos(α/2)|0⟩ + sin(α/2)|1⟩. RZ changes the relative complex phase, turning the vector around its z axis.

Each of the four layers repeats the eight input rotations, adds eight learned rotations, then applies the ordered CNOT ring. A CNOT toggles the target’s computational bit when its control is 1. It can entangle the state; it does not rotate a single local Bloch vector independently.

The readout uses seven Z-product expectations. Their weighted sum plus a learned bias becomes a score through σ(z) = 1/(1 + e⁻ᶻ). Training optimized quantum angles and this classical readout using labelled windows. The visual descriptors, selected size, threshold and local peak suppression remain classical.

Two reflections: equations & sources
Why two reflections produce a rotation ↓

The search begins with equal amplitudes aⱼ = 1/√N. The learned predicate selects M addresses; the oracle applies O|j⟩ = (−1)ᶠ⁽ʲ⁾|j⟩. Squaring removes the sign, so this first step leaves every probability unchanged.

The diffuser D = 2|s⟩⟨s| − I reflects each post-oracle amplitude about their mean: a′ⱼ = 2ā − aⱼ. Together these two reflections rotate the joint state by 2θ in the marked/unmarked plane, where θ = asin√(M/N).

After r complete rounds, P(accepted) = sin²((2r+1)θ). The optimum is close to π/(4θ) − ½. More rounds can rotate past the target direction and lower the probability; use the round slider below to see this overshoot. False accepted addresses receive the same amplification as correct ones.

The ideal search makes O(√(N/M)) oracle calls when the quantum oracle is already available. This demo first scans all windows with a classical circuit simulator and then compiles its accepted set. It demonstrates amplification, without claiming a faster end-to-end image search.

Not measured.

The default uses linear scores and preserves narrow peaks. Optional boost brightens weak scores using score^0.35 and can exaggerate background clues. This model scores Wanda-specific descriptors; it does not rank the closest-looking people. Use the predicate board for actual acceptance.

Display controls only. Colors use the selected fixed exposure; they do not change the detector, oracle or sample.

The Wanda score view uses a peak-preserving Gaussian envelope: broad weak regions cannot dilute an isolated high score. Its halo width is a display choice, not uncertainty. The search display transitions from that envelope to a Gaussian view of Born probabilities; the default reaches 100% probability view at the final peak. Detector scores are not calibrated identity probabilities or semantic person-similarity scores. Grover amplifies accepted addresses; it does not spread between neighboring cells. Select an exact map or hover for unsmoothed values.

Evidence, experiments & limitations
THE ACTUAL MODEL / REPRODUCIBLE EVIDENCE

Learned angles. Measured limits.

This browser uses a separately trained Wanda circuit. Classical stripe and palette descriptors prepare its inputs; the circuit and readout learn their window decision. The descriptors do not detect people or measure semantic resemblance. Recognition scans all candidate windows before simulated Grover begins.

Loading Wanda’s circuit…

Separate Chromium rendering audit: 15/15 target probes at the former default placement (276,348) passed across the original five unseeded worlds and supplied heights 40/52/64px; all five 52px empty-scene controls abstained. These are engineering probes, not a new statistical holdout. Native rendering passed 13/15 of the same target probes. This historical audit does not cover the newly curated Park variant. Pixels differed in every paired frame, and accepted sets agreed in 18/20. Browser resizing affects scores; the native reserved result above does not transfer automatically. The model and threshold stayed frozen. Read the paired audit ↓

Four classifier qubits and the default twelve location qubits serve different jobs. The circuit scores a window; Grover amplifies a compiled accepted-address oracle. This simulation does not establish an end-to-end quantum speedup or broad person recognition.

Park’s planted lookalike: a curated visual challenge ↓

Park includes a bystander derived from Wanda’s PNG, with a different outfit. Her actual image pixels pass through the same frozen QNN as every other window; no placement, mask or hand-assigned score enters inference. We selected this artwork with model feedback to create an illustrative near-match. This is curated demonstration art, not an independent recognition benchmark.

At the default supplied52px size, the planted person produces a70.21% detector peak, below the90.56% threshold, and the actual browser abstains with Wanda absent. Adding real Wanda at(420,300) yields one accepted address and the correct measured point. This is a conditional demonstration: supplied40px and46px searches falsely accept the lookalike. The QNN measures stripe and palette patterns, not person identity. Those failures and rejected artwork trials are retained. The historical reserved results above belong to the original unseeded scenes. Read the curation checks and failures ↓

Reproducibility & checkpoint metadata ↓

The trained checkpoint was frozen before the reserved test. Its inherited trainingDomain description contains an old artwork label; the explicit metadata erratum ↓ records the actual five-scene Wanda domain and the checkpoint hash. The numerical parameters, threshold, source freeze and measured results remain unchanged.

The model was fitted on new Wanda composites. Known-style visual descriptors and known target size are part of classical preparation. This is a controlled same-art experiment, with a matched classical baseline and retained failed searches.

Experiment: two identical Wandas ↓

The frozen QNN actually accepts both copies at (420,300) and (276,348). On the same 4,096-address lattice, the first useful Grover peak moves from round 50 with one accepted address to round 35 with two. At that peak each copy has about 49.9998% probability; the combined accepted probability is 99.9996848%. Their different QNN scores do not bias Grover: this oracle retains a yes/no predicate.

This is a controlled same-art experiment, separately checked in the real Chromium demo, with the model and threshold unchanged. The 10,000 seeded native samples split 4,987 / 5,013 between the two copies. No outcome was discarded. A tiny theoretical probability of an unmarked sample remains. These are demonstrations, not new reserved accuracy results.

What powered the historical QNN? ↓

Every default window score evaluates the saved variational quantum circuit. Both its quantum rotations and classical readout were optimized on labelled image windows. Classical pixel features prepare the inputs, and classical peak suppression keeps nearby duplicate detections together. The template matcher is a separately selected comparison; it does not gate or repair the default QNN. The circuit and Grover search are simulated in the browser.

Recognition still evaluates the candidate windows classically using circuit simulation before Grover starts. This experiment demonstrates a trained hybrid quantum classifier whose classical scores define a simulated Grover oracle, with no established end-to-end quantum speedup.

CLASSICAL TEMPLATE COMPARISON

The earlier matcher.
Separate evidence.

The earlier template matcher on the same whole-object bands was checked with 205 predefined placements across Festival, Arena and Queue. At a fixed 52px target and 64 × 64 grid, the matcher locates 117/194 targets above the 1% visibility gate; 77 visible placements are missed. Eleven less-visible cases abstain. No incorrect point is accepted, and all three target-free images reconstruct the background exactly and abstain.

These are controlled placements of the same supplied PNG, including deliberately difficult band crossings. They test the pixel predicate, not independent recognition accuracy. The 27 stored bands exactly reproduce their 44 source cutouts. Color contrast, smoothing and display crossfades do not change the accepted set or simulated sampling.

Earlier painting benchmark & its limits ↓

The earlier frozen audit uses the final striped PNG and the two archived public-domain paintings. These figures do not evaluate the new crowd scenes or automatic depth. At the default 52px target height and 64 × 64 grid, the matcher locates 48/48 clean placements and 45/47 visible nominal layered placements. In a harder set deliberately placed behind foreground objects, it locates only 13/34 visible targets.

Across all 2,064 probes, no incorrect point was marked. All 24 empty scenes and 57 fully hidden cases abstain. Visible targets can still be missed: 1,548/1,983 visible probes locate the target across the mixed sizes, grids and layer conditions. These are controlled placements of the same assets, rendered with Native Canvas; browser rasterization and new images may differ.

TEST THE WHOLE SCENE

Fragments can defeat the predicate.

The frozen QNN marks a true tile in 356/384 nominal 4 × 4 probes and 345/384 nominal 8 × 8 probes in a larger controlled audit. Both suites have zero false marks. These are Pillow-rendered placements of the same character and crowd, including dense boundary probes. The nominal 8 × 8 set has 369 unique geometry configurations among 384 predefined probes; repeated corner configurations retain their declared weighting.

Under separate scale and brightness stress, the 8 × 8 suite has only 132/384 clean-hit scenes: at least one true mark and no false marks. The matched logistic classifier also struggles, with 189/384 clean hits. These scene counts differ from patch accuracy and from a sampled quantum result.

✳

From a bus to a person-shaped target.

The same search mathematics can amplify different visual predicates. Locating a fictional figure in these controlled scenes is an educational example; broader person localization needs independent data and a reliable recognition oracle.

Compare the crowd and schoolbus demos by oracle quality, candidate count, and true-target probability. This project demonstrates no end-to-end quantum speedup.

03

Recognition supplies the question.
Interference changes the odds.

Three steps connect the image to the quantum experiment.

A

Learn the visual predicate

The default QNN angle-encodes eight color, stripe, centering and supplied-size features for each image window into four qubits. Trained rotations and entangling gates produce seven expectations; a learned readout scores the window. Threshold-passing peaks define the oracle. Inference receives final pixels and selected size, with no placement labels or clean-background reference.

qθ(xj) → threshold + local peaks → f(j)
B

Mark phase, then interfere

The oracle flips accepted regions’ amplitudes. Diffusion reflects every amplitude around their mean.

Of|j⟩ = (−1)f(j)|j⟩
a′j = 2ā − aj
C

Measure one region

For M accepted regions out of N, the ideal accepted-set probability follows an exact curve. False positives are amplified too.

P(r) = sin²[(2r + 1)θ]
θ = arcsin√(M/N)
